Items.Authors: Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Olivier Guyon, Victor Gasho, Douglas M. Kelly, Adam Fletcher, John Ford, Tommy Salanski, Maggie Kautz, Olivier F. Durney, Jamison Noenickx, Logan Pearce, Jay Kueny, Alycia Weinberger, Joseph D Long, Eden McEwen, Katie Twitchell, Joshua Liberman, Tiffany Nguyen, Adam Kraus, Jason Wang, Parker Johnson, Miles Lucas, Elena Tonucci, Rico Landman
Items.Title: The final design of GMagAO-X: high-contrast imaging at first-light of the GMT
Items.Abstract: GMagAO-X will be the first-light high-contrast imager on the 25 m Giant Magellan Telescope. The driving science case for GMagAO-X is characterization of the atmospheres of nearby rocky exoplanets such as Proxima Centauri b. This, and many more science cases will be enabled by a 21,000 actuator extreme adaptive optics (ExAO) system, an integrated coronagraphic wavefront control system with dedicated deformable mirrors, and a suite of imagers and spectrographs. GMagAO-X is on track to be ready at first-light of the GMT in the mid 2030s. We will provide an updated overview of the instrument designed to achieve our ambitious performance targets and the resultant expected scientific yield. We will discuss the results of risk reduction activities and prototyping. We will also briefly review progress towards demonstrating scaled performance targets with the recently commissioned MagAO-X on the 6.5 m Clay Telescope.

Items.Authors: Michel Tallon, Clémentine Béchet, Isaac Dinis, Florian Ferreira, Paul Fontanillas, Nicolas Galland, Charles Goulas, Markus Kasper, Caroline Kulcsár, Jalo Nousiainen, Henri-François Raynaud, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Éric Thiébaut, Maud Langlois, Anthony Boccaletti, Emiliano Diolaiti, Raphaël Galicher, Miska Le Louarn, Magali Loupias, Johan Mazoyer, Julien Milli, Laura Schreiber, Fabrice Vidal, Gaële Barbary, François Wildi
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: a review of six selected control algorithms and the results achieved to date
Items.Abstract: SAXO+ is the second-stage adaptive optics (AO) system to be inserted in cascade after SPHERE extreme AO at the VLT, aiming to improve coronagraphic contrast closer to the star and enable observations of fainter, redder stars. This leads to the use of a modulated pyramid wavefront sensor and a twice as fast AO loop. A classical optimal modal-gain integrator is the baseline control algorithm. We test five alternative algorithms offering prediction to mitigate delay, improved reconstruction, or better tolerance to PyWFS non-linearities. Three are based on linear estimation methods (Linear Quadratic Gaussian, data-driven, and iterative minimum-variance reconstructor) and two use neural networks and reinforcement learning (Policy Optimization for AO and Dual-stage Supervised & Reinforcement Learning). So all employ machine learning. Algorithms are compared with the COMPASS simulator, modeling two cascaded AO. On-sky tests with the RTC COSMIC will validate final performance and operability.

Items.Authors: Marco Bartolini, Snehal Ujjainkar
Items.Title: evolution of the SKA observatory software architecture, from design to implementation
Items.Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA) project initially defined a software architecture during its design phase, structured around telescope elements and consortia responsibilities. These designs captured each element’s architecture at a high level of abstraction, focusing on key design choices. This paper examines how the SKA software architecture has evolved in response to construction-phase realities. We identify and analyse major gaps revealed during implementation, describe the trade-offs and decisions made to address them, and show how ongoing development activities are shaping the concrete architecture deployed today. The paper also presents the current state of the software design, reflects on lessons learned, and outlines the remaining challenges and future directions for the observatory’s software implementation.

Items.Authors: Louis Desdoigts
Items.Title: From Sparse Pupils to Differentiable Instruments: The Evolving Legacy of Aperture Masking Interferometry
Items.Abstract: Aperture Masking Interferometry (AMI) has played an unusual role in diffraction-limited astronomy. Although often viewed as a specialised high-angular-resolution mode for residual phase errors, its broader legacy lies in the calibration methods and instruments it generated. This talk takes a methodological perspective on AMI: not only as an observing mode, but as a calibration-driven approach to high-contrast imaging inside the classical diffraction limit. I will discuss how interferometric calibration led to kernel phase, photonic remapping, and mask concepts like Jewel. I will focus on the JWST aperture mask, whose calibration challenges provided a proving ground for differentiable modelling and led to AMIGO. I will discuss future tools from this next generation, including detector calibration and calibrator-free interferometry. AMI’s impact lies not only in its science, but in the instrumental and methodological legacy it seeded across diffraction-limited astronomy.

Items.Authors: Gregory Y. Prigozhin, Marshall Bautz, Beverly LaMarr, Kevan Donlon, Christopher Leitz, Eric Miller, Michelle Gabutti, Jill Juneau, Sven Herrmann, Peter Orel, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Michael Cooper, Noah Pestana, Doug Yang, Ilya Prigozhin, Abigail Pan, Haley Stueber, Declan O'Neill, Glenn Morris, Steven Allen
Items.Title: Noise and charge transfer characteristics of Fast, Low-noise CCD Sensors for AXIS
Items.Abstract: A new CCD for the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS), has been designed by the MIT Lincoln Laboratories. The device called CCID100 serves as a form/fit/function prototype for future X-ray missions and has a classic Frame Transfer architecture with 16 parallel output channels allowing for fast readout of the entire 1450x1455 24 micron pixel array. It is built on a high resistivity substrate with a single layer polysilicon gates and low noise pJFET outputs. As a part of a collaborative effort by MIT Kavli Institute and Stanford University, we have built a test camera that allows to evaluate the devices in a wide temperature range. Here we present the results of device testing, focusing mostly on charge transfer inefficiency (CTI) dependencies on frequency, clock amplitudes and temperature, and studying of detector noise as a function of multiple operational parameters. We utilized the device charge injection capability as a powerful tool for characterizing

Items.Authors: Christian J. Killow, Robert G. Bell, Andrew Boyd, James Copley, James N. Monks, Manish R. Patel, Ryan Swindell, Gavin Wedlock, Jonathan Williams, Jon P. Mason
Items.Title: The optical head for the Dust Environment Spectral Imager (DESI) on Lightship-1
Items.Abstract: We present the optical system design of the Dust Environment Spectral Imager (DESI), an instrument that will fly on LightShip-1 planned for launch in the early 2030's.    DESI will take full-disk multispectral images of Mars with 5 km resolution from the UV to visible. This enables monitoring of Martian dust, water ice clouds and ozone that will generate new scientific data in a variety of important areas, including weather forecasting.    A single optical channel has been designed to operate across the wavebands with eight bandpass filters to select wavelengths of interest within this spectrum.    Optical and coating design at such short wavelengths poses considerable challenges due to the truncated material choices suitable for use in the deep UV. Added to the practical limitations of space flight optics, novel designs were needed.

Items.Authors: Jason E. Austermann, The CCAT Collaboration
Items.Title: CCAT: The focal plane arrays of the prime-cam submillimeter receiver
Items.Abstract: Prime-Cam is a multi-instrument receiver for the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST). Prime-Cam hosts 7 independent instrument modules with unique focal planes that are designed and optimized for complementary mapping and spectral abilities. Each focal plane consists of large-format arrays of feedhorn-coupled microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKIDs). When completed, Prime-Cam will contain over 100,000 MKIDs. Here we describe the designs, fabrication, and in-lab characterizations of completed deployment devices for each of four initial instrument modules. We compare and contrast the unique and differing design elements of each focal plane. We review available in-lab performance, and discuss yield and uniformity metrics for completed deployment arrays. We also describe the design, fabrication, and performance of the silicon-platelet feedhorn arrays used in most of the focal planes, including the very first silicon feedhorn arrays to operate fully in the submillimeter.

Items.Authors: Solange Ramírez, Maren Cosens, Nicholas P. Konidaris, Francisco Garzón, Brian McLeod, Suzanne Ramsay, Leon Aslan, Robert Barkhouser, Christoph Birk, Julia Brady, Tyson Hare, Stephen C. Hope, Charlie Hull, Karim Kaismoune, Daniel D. Kelson, Gerrad Killion, Alicia Lanz, Jacob McCloskey, Andrew B. Newman, Gwen C. Rudie, William Schoenell, Patricio Schurter, Stephen A. Smee, Jason E. Williams
Items.Title: Community lessons from builders of infrared multi-object spectrographs
Items.Abstract: We present a summary of lessons learned from our community on the design and construction of infrared multi-object spectrographs. As members of the Magellan Infrared Multi-Object Spectrograph (MIRMOS) development team, we were motivated to learn about the most common troubles faced by our colleagues and incorporate measures in our design and assembly plan to address known issues. The lessons are compiled as a result of interviews we carried out with members of the instrument development teams for several multi-object infrared spectrographs. We found considerable overlap in the lessons learned for building this type of instrument; many of which relate to the cryogenic operation of the instruments. In this paper, we will present the compilation of general and specific lessons which we found relevant for the successful development of MIRMOS or any other future cryogenic instruments.

Items.Authors: John Franklin Crenshaw, Hurum Maksora Tohfa, Peter Xiangyuan Ma, Andrew J. Connolly, J. Bryce Kalmbach, Krzysztof Suberlak, Josh Bloom, Keith Bechtol, Merlin Fisher-Levine, Craig S. Lage, Guillem Megias Homar, Joshua E. Meyers, Rebekah Polen, Bruno C. Quint, Andrew P. Rasmussen, Tiago Ribeiro, Aaron Roodman, Eli S. Rykoff, David Sanmatrim, Theo Schutt, Will Sutherland, Sandrine J. Thomas, Elana K. Urbach
Items.Title: Deploying AI for active optics control of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Vera C.~Rubin Observatory uses an active optics system (AOS) to deliver consistently high image quality across its 9.6\,deg$^2$ field of view. The baseline forward-modeling approach provides physically interpretable wavefront fits, but challenges the cadence required for LSST. We describe two AI-based methods for accelerating wavefront inference: AIDonut, a neural-network replacement for the wavefront-estimation step, and TARTS, a larger framework that incorporates donut detection and sensor-level aggregation. Both systems are trained on Rubin simulations and adapted to Rubin commissioning data through transfer learning, using supervised and unsupervised approaches. Early validation in on-sky tests shows both models converge to image quality and alignment consistent with the forward-modeling baseline. These demonstrations are an important step towards fast, AI-assisted active optics control for Rubin.

Items.Authors: Brandon D. Chalifoux, Brody D. McElwain, Hill R. Tailor, Sofia Hillman, Dillan B. Synan
Items.Title: Development of flex modules for high-resolution thin X-ray telescope mirrors
Items.Abstract: Flex Modules have potential for sub-arcsecond resolution with sub-mm thick mirrors, offering vast improvements on both resolution and throughput over existing X-ray telescopes. Flex Modules are composed of stacks of Flex Segments that are simultaneously figured and aligned after they are coated, assembled, and bonded into the module. Ultrafast laser stress figuring (ULSF) is the key process step enabling this final-step figuring, but many other process steps are necessary to fabricate, and ultimately manufacture, Flex Modules. In this talk, I will describe our ongoing technology development efforts toward fabricating and assembling Flex Segments into Flex Modules.

Items.Authors: Gregory Mace, Sungho Lee, Alycia J. Weinberger, Cynthia Brooks, Sanghyuk Kim, Woojin Park, Heeyoung Oh, Hanshin Lee, John M. Good, Cooper W. Dix, Kyle Kaplan, Karina Leppik, Ueejeong Jeong, Erica Sawczynec, Michelle Grigas, Shiang-Yu Wang, Po-Chieh Yu, Chueh-Yi Chou, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Jae-Joon Lee, Moo-Young Chun, Jae Sok Oh, Jae-Rim Koo, Hyeon Cheol Seong, Ho-Gyu Lee, Sang-Mok Cha, Biho Jang, Kyohoon Ahn, Young Sam Yu, Chan Park, Byeong-Gon Park, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: the Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph final design phase
Items.Abstract: GMTNIRS is a high-resolution spectrograph that will cover 1.08-5.4 μm in a single exposure with R=65,000 in the J, H, and K bands and R=80,000 in the L and M bands. As a first-generation adaptive-optics (AO) instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope, GMTNIRS will have a 60mas wide and 1.35 arcsecond long slit. The GMTNIRS design is evolving in response to emerging science problems, particularly in the area of exoplanet atmospheres. Risks related to immersion grating development, volume phase holographic transmission grating procurement, and camera manufacture have been retired. The high efficiency of our double-side coated silicon grisms (deployed in JWST) motivates the use of transmissive cross-dispersers at L and M. We will report on the optimization of the instrument design for the technical demands of both GMT and Magellan and update the community on the Final Design Phase of development for GMTNIRS.

Items.Authors: Solal Thomas, Pierre Albart, Christian Bastin, Jonathan De Ville, Carlo Flebus, Eric Gabriel, Grégory P. Lousberg, Laurence Méant, Sabrina Orban, Olivier Pirnay, Jean-Marc Tortolani
Items.Title: DAG 4m Telescope: on-sky alignment and commissioning
Items.Abstract: The 4-meter class telescope of the Eastern Anatolia Observatory (DAG400), designed and built by AMOS is a f/14 Ritchey-Chrétien with two Nasmyth foci and active optics system controlling the primary mirror shape and the secondary and tertiary mirrors position.  Following the telescope erection on-site and optics integration, the final tests encompassed fine alignment and ultimately performance assessment on-sky. Advanced alignment techniques such as wavefront-curvature sensing and coma-free point adjustment were employed to achieve diffraction-limited performance in optical and near-infrared bands. On-sky tests, complemented by lucky-imaging methods, confirmed excellent image quality, pointing accuracy, and tracking stability.   This paper details the on-site installation steps, alignment procedures, and final performance results, demonstrating the readiness of the DAG telescope for scientific operations.

Items.Authors: Haley R. Stueber, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Peter Orel, Steven W. Allen, Marshall W. Bautz, Michael Cooper, Kevan Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, Sven Herrmann, Jill Juneau, Beverly J. LaMarr, Christopher Leitz, Eric D. Miller, Glenn Morris, Declan O'Neill, Abigail Y. Pan, Tonya L. Peshel, Artem Poliszczuk, Gregory Y. Prigozhin, Keith Warner
Items.Title: High-speed, low-noise, multi-megapixel CCDs for next generation x-ray observatories
Items.Abstract: Next generation X-ray observatories require fast, low-noise, low-power, multi-megapixel imaging spectrometers. To meet these demands, the X-ray Astronomy and Observational Cosmology (XOC) Group at Stanford, in partnership with the MIT Kavli Institute and MIT Lincoln Laboratory (MIT-LL), is developing multi-channel X-ray charge-coupled devices (CCDs) and fast readout architectures. We report the energy resolution and noise performance achieved with a full-scale (1440x1440-pixel), 16-channel, front-illuminated MIT-LL CCD detector developed for the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS) concept, the CCID-100, read out using two Multi-Channel Readout Chip (MCRC) ASICs in the new Stanford CCID-100 test setup. We describe an automated method for bias optimization on each CCD channel, and integrated debugging features of the front-end ASIC and readout system. The demonstrated performance confirms that these systems can meet the speed and noise requirements of future strategic X-ray missions.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo König, Tobias Wenger, Niyati Desai, Dimitri Mawet, Eugene Serabyn
Items.Title: Prototype advancements of scalar metasurface phase masks for high-contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory concept (HWO) requires a coronagraph reaching contrast on the order of 1e-10 across a broad band. One promising approach to achieve this requirement is to use a scalar implementation of a vortex coronagraph. Metasurfaces are a promising technology for achromatizing scalar phase masks such as the vortex, because they allow for more design freedom in a single layer of constant thickness compared to scalar phase masks based on variable thickness of a dielectric substrate. We here present our recent prototype advancement of scalar metasurface phase masks. This includes phase metrology and contrast measurements of various phase mask topographies implemented with our silicon-based metasurface framework for the near-IR. We conclude with the next steps needed to push the performance of these masks towards deeper contrast levels required for future space telescope missions such as HWO.

Items.Authors: Katie Twitchell, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Olivier Guyon, Jennifer Lumbres, Lauren Schatz, Alexander D. Hedglen, Joseph D. Long, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Eden A. McEwen, Avalon L. McLeod, Joshua Liberman, Parker T. Johnson, Miles Lucas, Elena Tonucci, Matthijs Mars
Items.Title: Closed-loop atmospheric dispersion correction for high contrast imaging with MagAO-X
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric dispersion causes elongation of the broadband PSF of ground-based telescopes, especially in the visible spectrum. This results in degraded image quality alongside reduced coronagraph light-blocking efficiency, both of which limit high-contrast observations. Dispersive optics known as Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors (ADCs) are used to compensate for this effect, but uncertainties in the analytical models which typically control them often lead to over- or under-correction of the true atmospheric dispersion. In this work, we present a method of closed-loop ADC control using the Magellan Extreme Adaptive Optics system MagAO-X and demonstrate real-time correction of residual atmospheric dispersion on-sky. Active atmospheric dispersion correction on MagAO-X is a precursor to high-contrast imaging for the upcoming Extremely Large Telescopes, where high-precision dispersion compensation will be required to image exoplanets in reflected light.

Items.Authors: Narsireddy Anugu, John D. Monnier, Stefan Kraus, Robert Klement, Gail H. Schaefer, Douglas R. Gies
Items.Title: On-sky demonstration of dual-field interferometry at the CHARA Array
Items.Abstract: We report an on-sky demonstration of dual-field interferometry at the CHARA Array, a capability inspired by the dual-beam architecture of VLTI/GRAVITY and designed to expand CHARA’s sensitivity, astrometric precision, and scientific reach. Our approach uses MIRC-X (H-band) and MYSTIC (K-band) beam combiners in a paired configuration, where one instrument operates as a real-time fringe tracker while the other records long-exposure science fringes on a second target within the 5″ interferometric field of view. The roles of the two instruments are interchangeable, enabling dual-field operation across a wide wavelength range J/H/K. Dual-field fringes were first obtained in summer 2025 on the bright wide binary system α Piscium, marking the first demonstration of off-axis fringe tracking at CHARA. Our goals include extending this mode to faint-target interferometry, enabling long-exposure coherent integrations on stars several magnitudes fainter than the real-time fringe-tracking limit.

Items.Authors: Abigail Y. Pan, Declan O'Neill, Kevan Donlon, Peter Orel, Sven Herrmann, Steven W. Allen, Marshall W. Bautz, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Michael Cooper, Catherine E. Grant, Jill Juneau, Chris Leitz, Beverly LaMarr, Eric D. Miller, Glenn Morris, Tonya L. Peshel, Artem Poliszczuk, Gregory Prigozhin, Ilya Prigozhin, Haley R. Stueber, Keith Warner
Items.Title: First results for second generation SiSeRO CCD devices
Items.Abstract: The Astro2020 Decadal recommended the development of a suite of next generation astronomical observatories spanning the X-ray to near-IR spectrum. These programs require fast, extremely low noise detectors to fulfill their science goals. To address this technology gap, Stanford X-ray Astronomy and Observational Cosmology (XOC) group, MIT Lincoln Laboratory (MIT-LL), and MIT Kavli Institute (MKI) are advancing Single electron Sensitive Read Out (SiSeRO), a multiband detector technology capable of achieving substantially sub-electron noise via Repetitive Non-Destructive Readout (RNDR). We present initial results for our second generation SiSeRO CCDs. We also discuss our test bed, including a readout electronics system capable of accommodating all second-generation SiSeRO CCD variants utilizing the XOC-designed Multi-Channel Readout Chip (MCRC) ASIC.

Items.Authors: Tristen M. Sextro, James H. Tutt, Randall L. McEntaffer, Alexandra N. Higley, Ross C. McCurdy, Andrew D. Holland, Daniel Evan, Karen Holland, David Gopinath
Items.Title: Electron multiplying CCDs as soft X-ray detectors for the Pathfinder Off-Plane Grating Rocket Experiment
Items.Abstract: The Pathfinder Off-plane Grating Rocket Experiment (OGRE-P) plans to use Electron-Multiplying CCDs (EMCCDs) as detectors. EMCCDs incorporate an additional gain register to amplify the photoelectron signal before readout, increasing sensitivity by suppressing readout noise making them ideal for low-light X-ray imaging. The EMCCDs used are developed by Teledyne e2v with OGRE camera and electronics made by XCAM and Open University. The mission consists of four EMCCDs; three for spectral data collection and the fourth in the center of the focal plane. Promising results have been found using of EMCCDs as soft X-ray detectors for OGRE with measurements of the detector energy resolution over emission lines covering our bandpass (0.3-1.2keV). Spectral resolution has been measured over varying gain and temperature to analyze its impact on performance. Predictions of detector performance have been simulated given detector characteristics to show sensitivity to the expected Capella spectrum.

Items.Authors: Tristan Buey, Eitan Péchevis, Jean-Michel Reess, Marion Bonafous, Jérôme Parisot, Didier Zeganadin, Martin Pertenais, Ingo Walter, Ana-Catalina Plesa, Giulia Alemanno, Pascal Huguet-Chantome, Anthony Juin, Jérôme Carron, Matthieu Tatat, Martial Culie
Items.Title: Design, performances, and qualification of the optics of the Venus Spectrometer Instrument (VEM)
Items.Abstract: The concept of the optical objective of the VEM instrument (Venus Mapper under DLR responsibility for VERITAS and EnVision missions) will be shown with the first results of its measured performances.  Academic partners (LIRA and DLR) are associated with industrial partners (Bertin-Winlight, Cilas and MECANO-ID) with the CNES support.  Robust design with 3 lenses and filter all integrated in a mechanical barrel has successfully passed the first review.  The mechanical models and FEA results will be presented.  The whole qualification process and the facilities developed at LIRA will be exposed.

Items.Authors: Matteo De Magistris, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Monica Rainer, Giorgio Pariani, Luca Oggioni, Simone Doniselli, Marco Riva, Alessio Zanutta, Paolo Di Marcantonio, Matteo Aliverti, Edoardo Redaelli, Chiara Selmi, Lorenzo Cabona, Igor Coretti
Items.Title: ANDES, the high resolution spectrograph for the ELT: systems engineering activities for the preparation of the ANDES Fibre Routing Delta- PDR, part of the ANDES Fibre Link subsystem
Items.Abstract: This work provides a system-level description of the Fibre Routing module of ANDES, part of the Fibre Link subsystem, together with the IFU module, which won't be discussed here. This module is responsible for feeding the spectrographs of ANDES with the various sources of light, scientific or calibration.   The development of the Fibre Routing module follows a sequential design that starts from its functional black-box analysis, identifying the objectives and the external interactions, and continues with its internal functional and physical analysis. Following this approach, all elements composing the module have a technical justification in the design, which can be easily retrieved using the traceability capabilities provided by the MBSE model of this module. As a direct consequence of this design procedure, both the external and internal interfaces of the Fibre Routing module are clearly identified and managed.

Items.Authors: Stephen D. Bongiorno
Items.Title: Development of replicated epoxy ceramic X-ray optics
Items.Abstract: The observation of astrophysical X-rays is critically important for understanding the universe. In pursuit of developing large effective area, high-angular resolution X-ray optics for astrophysics, we are developing a Replicated Epoxy Ceramic X-ray Optic (RECXO) technology to produce full-shell grazing-incidence replicated optics. Full-shell replicated X-ray optics offer unique advantages for a wide variety of missions, namely: (1) simplified manufacturing and reduced cost per effective area due to replication, (2) simplified assembly due to monolithic primary and secondary optical design, (3) cost-effective production of multi-mirror-module observatories which have improved high-energy response for a given focal length due to smaller graze angles, offer redundancy in the case of detector failure, and provide a platform for using different detectors simultaneously. In this paper we will present the RECXO concept, and current status of the development effort.

Items.Authors: Xiangyan Yuan, Zhongwen Hu, Chen Xu, Yi Zheng, Jinfeng Wang, Qishuai Lu, Dehua Yang, Zhongyu Yue, Bozhong Gu, Shihai Yang, Hua Bai, Kai Zhang, Hangxin Ji, Shun Li, Jifeng Liu, Xuefei Gong, Jinming Bai, Dongguang Wang, Liang Ge, Lu Feng
Items.Title: Development of the 14.5-meter Optical/Infrared Telescope
Items.Abstract: The 14.5-meter telescope programme was approved in 2024 which will significantly mitigate the demands of China’s astronomical community for 10-m class large-aperture optical/infrared telescope. The telescope will be located in the top astronomical sites with very good seeing conditions in Lenghu Qinghai province and is designed as a general-purpose telescope for a wide range of frontier astrophysics and astrometry research. The primary mirror consists of 120 hexagonal segments with a nominal circumscribed diameter of 1.44 meters. The unvignetting field of view (FOV) is 15 arcminute and the f-ratio 14.5. According to the current schedule,, the telescope structure and control system will be completed in 2028 and the mirrors will be installed at the telescope starting from the late 2028 and finished all in 2030 together with three first generation science instruments.

Items.Authors: Woojin Kim, Bongkon Moon, Dukhang Lee, Dae-Hee Lee, Minsup Jeong, Yunjong Kim, Jihun Kim, Jehyuck Shin, Seul-Min Baek, Mingyeong Lee, Sung-Joon Park, Chae Kyung Sim
Items.Title: Flight Model development and system verification of the GrainCams payload for the CLPS lunar rover
Items.Abstract: The Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, a component of NASA’s Artemis program, supports lunar exploration by enabling the delivery of scientific instruments to the Moon through commercial lander missions. GrainCams is a candidate payload developed by the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute (KASI), consisting of SurfCam and LevCam to study micro-scale regolith structures and lofted dust near the lunar surface. This presentation introduces the objectives and system design of GrainCams, highlighting its role in advancing surface science investigations on future lunar exploration missions.

Items.Authors: Randall K. Smith, Peter N. Cheimets
Items.Title: A new approach to precision X-ray optics for next-generation observatories
Items.Abstract: We describe a fabrication process designed to produce assembled and aligned X-ray mirrors that is cost-effective, manufacturable, and suitable for the next generation of X-ray observatories such as Lynx. Our top considerations for the mirror design and process development are sub-arcsecond angular resolution, industrial scalability, and overall simplicity. All of the processes required in our approach have been individually demonstrated, typically as part of existing commercial production. Our approach applies a collection of these techniques to fabricate grazing incidence X-ray mirrors, and then accurately mount them in a support structure to demonstrate the entire process in a testable fashion.

Items.Authors: Tayyaba Zafar, Jonathan Lawrence, Alexander Ji, Scott M. Croom, Sarah Martell, Steven L. Finkelstein, Michael Goodwin, Jessica Zheng, Vitor N. Hartmann, Celestina S. Lacombe, Umme T. Ahmed, Benjamin Courtney-Barrer, Anilkumar Mailvaganam, Tamal Mukherjee, Imam U. Aalia, Samuel Carlson, Arihant Raidani, Bahareh S. Salmasi, Xuanyi Lyu, Matthew Colless, Andrew M. Hopkins, Magda Arnaboldi, Celine Peroux, Warren R. Brown, Charlie Conroy, Zhemin Cai, Srivardini Ayyappan, Dian Pipit Triani, Helen McGregor
Items.Title: Expanding GMT’s discovery space: MANIFEST science cases for the next decade
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) will deliver transformative science through its unprecedented collecting area. MANIFEST, the fibre-positioning system for GMT, maximises this potential by enabling highly multiplexed spectroscopy across a wide field of view. This talk will present key science drivers for MANIFEST, including mapping the Milky Way and Local Group galaxies, dwarf galaxies, spatially resolved studies of galaxies up to cosmic noon, and galaxies at the edge of reionisation. We will further highlight recent updates on MANIFEST include multi-mode operations, the exposure time calculator, and IFU-multiplexing modes for GCLEF and GMACS. These capabilities will empower astronomers to tackle fundamental questions on star formation, dark matter, and the baryon cycle, ensuring readiness for GMT’s first-light era.

Items.Authors: Rodrigo G. Freundt, Baird Bankovic, Thomas Nikola, Gordon Stacey, Michael Niemack
Items.Title: CCAT: In-lab characterization of the EoR-Spec instrument module
Items.Abstract: The Epoch of Reionization Spectrometer (EoR-Spec) is an upcoming Line Intensity Mapping instrument for the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope. EoR-Spec will be installed in early 2027 on the Prime-Cam modular receiver alongside existing 280 GHz and 350 GHz cameras. The addition of a scanning Fabry-Perot Interferometer to the optical system is what enables wide-field spectral imaging with a broadband direct-detection camera, featuring a spectral resolution of R~100 across the 210-420 GHz sub-mm sky. With more than 6000 Kinetic Inductance Detectors, we aim to make a 3D map of the redshifted ionized carbon line emission from z = 3.5 to 8 by integrating for ~4000 hours on the E-COSMOS and E-CDFS fields. Here we give an update on the status of the instrument, including in-lab characterization of the detector arrays, as well as validation of the spectral scanning mechanism and observing strategies for first light science.

Items.Authors: Claire Lamour, Guillaume Foucaud, Philippe Wuillaume, Thibaud Marchand, Nicolas Verbrugge, Claire Li, Emilien Harmand, Elodie Milhiet, Romain Meunier, Thomas Yoo
Items.Title: ELT M5 Manufacturing and testing status
Items.Abstract: In 2019, the European Southern Observatory (ESO) awarded a contract for the manufacturing of the fifth mirror for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) to Safran Reosc. The ELT M5 Mirror, measuring 2.7 m × 2.2 m, will be the world's largest tip-tilt mirror and one of the largest Silicon Carbide with Chemical Vapour Deposition (SiC-CVD) brazed mirror.   M5 presents unique and significant challenges due to its large size, reduced edge margins, complex thickness management, material homogeneity issues, susceptibility to bending and quilting effects, brazed joints, and stringent wavefront error (WFE) specifications. These factors combine to make both polishing and metrology highly demanding.  To address these challenges, a dedicated polishing station has been established, along with a specialized WFE test bench that enables rapid and automatic measurements to nanometer-level precision.   This presentation will detail the methods employed and present the latest results achieved on the M5 mirror.

Items.Authors: Anna MacIver, Miguel Angel Cagigas García, Paula Bañares-Palacios, Elvio Hernández Suárez, Rafael Melgar Hernandez, Stephen Todd, Amelia Calderhead, Elizabeth George, Alberto Hernández-González, Eduard Muslimov
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: a dynamic systems engineering approach for rescoping the HARMONI integral field spectrograph
Items.Abstract: HARMONI, the first-light near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT, underwent a major rescope in 2024–2025 to simplify a complex cryogenic architecture while preserving science capability. The paper describes how systems engineering processes were adapted and applied for accelerated decision-making under schedule and budget constraints. Tools such as compliance matrices, complexity scoring, FMECA, and risk-based prototyping were applied iteratively to identify non-compliances, prioritise risks, and evaluate architectural trade-offs. This dynamic approach resulted in a system with reduced mechanism complexity, improved WCS stability, and improved performance, demonstrating how agile systems engineering can manage design evolution in large-scale instrumentation projects.

Items.Authors: Amanda Arvai, Margaret Jordan, Christopher Trinh
Items.Title: Optimizing Science Efficiency on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope
Items.Abstract: Observation time on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is a valuable astrophysics resource. This paper will provide an overview of how the science and flight operations prime contractor Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) in Baltimore Maryland, under the direction of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, seeks to optimize JWST science operational efficiency through a process of continuous improvement. It will provide evidence of tangible efficiency improvements, including a 6% increase in time spent in science visits. It will also detail improvements to science productivity, such as additional parallel observation capabilities and new science modes. Together, these improvements maximize the scientific output of JWST while also keeping it aligned with the evolving needs of the scientific community.

Items.Authors: Pau Ramos, Konstantin Ryabinin, Ryou Ohsawa, Wolfgang Löffler, Yoshiyuki Yamada, Daisuke Kawata, Michael Biermann
Items.Title: The JASMINE astrometric flexible block iterative solver (JAXBIS): concept and verification with full-mission sized mock data
Items.Abstract: The upcoming Japan Astrometry Satellite Mission for Infrared Exploration (JASMINE) will provide proper motions and parallaxes for the highly obscured and reddened stars in the central-most parts of the Milky Way, which could help disentangle the origin of the different components that co-exist in the inner-most ~200pc. Since optical wavelengths are blocked by dust, JASMINE observes in the near infrared, a band for which high-precision astrometry is just becoming feasible. As such, extensive testing will be required to assess the performance of our models of the optics and detectors against different possible scenarios. We have designed an iterative Least Squares solver that can process billions of observations, millions of parameters, while relying on auto-differentiation to bypass the need to recalculate the analytical derivatives of our changing calibration models. In this contribution, we present in detail our novel software and the results of the first full-mission scale test.

Items.Authors: Maria Bazzicalupo, Giulia Carlà, Lorenzo Busoni, Nicolò Azzaroli, Alfio Puglisi
Items.Title: Laboratory validation of the CiaoCiao wavefront sensor for phase discontinuity detection in fragmented-pupil optical telescopes
Items.Abstract: The next generation of large ground-based telescopes, like the ELT, will have fragmented pupils due to thick spiders supporting the secondary mirror. This segmentation challenges adaptive optics (AO) systems, as wavefront sensors may fail to sense phase jumps across the spiders. To address this, we developed the CiaoCiao WFS, a rotational shearing interferometer designed to detect and quantify phase discontinuities. After promising simulations, we report its first experimental validation with a prototype assembled at the Arcetri Observatory. The setup includes a custom segmented mirror (“Pistonator”) to inject controlled piston and a Mach–Zehnder interferometer with a rotated Dove prism. Laboratory results show a linear response to differential piston. We also present tests with a deformable mirror and broadband light to evaluate performance under realistic AO residuals.

Items.Authors: Juan Francisco Márquez, Graciela Delgado-García, Horacio Rodríguez Delgado, Francisco J. Hernández, C.A.L. Segura, Jacinto Javier Vaz Cedillo, C. M. Gutiérrez, Alejandra Goded, David Copley, Adam Garner, Adrian McGrath, Helen Jermak, Iain Steele, César Rodríguez Pereira, Fernando Sánchez, Francisco Javier De Cos Juez, Miguel Torres, Alberto Prieto, César Quintana, Josué Barrera, Asier Oria-Carreras, Marta Escriche, Javier León-Gil, J. J. Fernández-Valdivia, Pablo Fuerte-Rodriguez
Items.Title: IAC contribution to the New Robotic Telescope: an overview
Items.Abstract: The New Robotic Telescope (NRT) is an ongoing project to build a fully autonomous 4-meter telescope, planned to begin operations around 2030, and optimized for rapid follow-up of a wide range of transient astronomical phenomena. Located at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory in La Palma, it is being developed by a consortium including the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC), Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), and the Universidad de Oviedo (UO). The IAC leads the development of the telescope-level control system and the design and development of the optical and optomechanical systems, including the segmented primary mirror (M1) and the secondary mirror (M2), along with studies of its operational behaviour, alignment, and long-term performance. This paper summarises the progress made so far, and highlights the ongoing developments and future steps and milestones identified for the project.

Items.Authors: Dustin K. Swarm, Casey T. DeRoo, Carolyn A. Kierans, Kirtan P. Dixit, Danielle N. Gurgew
Items.Title: Optimization and simulation of soft gamma-ray focusing optics
Items.Abstract: The soft gamma ray emission line at 511 keV traces electron-positron annihilation in our Galaxy. Due to the challenges of imaging the annihilation emission, the source of Galactic positrons remains an open question. An imaging telescope with angular resolution on the order of 1 arcmin will be necessary to identify and spatially resolve individual sources of Galactic positrons. Grazing-incidence focusing optics with multilayer mirror coatings could offer a promising technology pathway for achieving such an instrument. Here we discuss the optical design and multilayer formulation for a future 511 keV focusing imager. We present the optimization approach for multilayer coatings applied to replicated optics developed at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC). We predict instrument performance via ray tracing simulations and provide sensitivity estimates for appropriate gamma-ray detectors.

Items.Authors: Paolo Martini, Claudio Pernechele, Emanuele Simioni, Givanni Costa, Luca Girolimetto, Luigi Lessio, Emilio Banfi, Carlo Moroni, Letizia Scaciga, Diego Scaccabarozzi, Chiara Martina, Antonio Appiani
Items.Title: PANCAM Vision System: panoramic camera for planetary exploration; a NewSpace approach
Items.Abstract: The paper introduces the PANCAM Vision System, an integrated panoramic imaging and processing platform designed for future planetary exploration. Developed within the framework of the NewSpace era, the system prioritizes the use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components to minimize size, mass, and power without sacrificing scientific precision. Despite using commercial parts, the system undergoes strict Radiation Hardness Assurance through software simulation (extensive software modelling of particle fluxes and radiation effects (irradiation dose, single event effects) and heritage analysis (Evaluation of component production stability and prior space heritage). The PANCAM Vision System demonstrates that by applying precise engineering and rigorous qualification to COTS technology, space missions can achieve the cost and efficiency benefits of the NewSpace paradigm while maintaining high-level scientific capability.

Items.Authors: Aura Amorós Torné, Albert Tomàs Justribo, Miguel Redondo De Santos, Manuel Canchado, Oriol Casamor, Joan Manel Casalta Escuer, Michael Mueller, Yannick Lammen
Items.Title: Novel approaches for nanometre stability and seismic protection in the ESO ELT M2 and M3 Cells
Items.Abstract: The development and verification of the ESO Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) M2 and M3 Cells are nearing completion, representing a key milestone in the telescope’s opto-mechanical realisation. These systems, supporting and aligning 4-metre-class monolithic mirrors, faced unprecedented challenges through design, manufacturing, and verification. An earthquake mitigation system was developed to protect the 12-ton assemblies under seismic loads up to 4.8g RMS. The Positioning Stage achieves dynamic stability below 60 nm and 30 nrad, while the passive support ensures surface figure errors below 370 nm RMS across all operational conditions. Verification required novel metrology and tailored methodologies. The paper presents the main design innovations, verification results, and lessons learned.

Items.Authors: Gustav M. Pettersson, Gabor Furesz, Nathan P. Lourie, F. Elio Angile, Jill Juneau, Gerardo Berlanga Molina, Robert A. Simcoe
Items.Title: SuperFIRE: Concept evolution of a seeing-limited broadband spectrograph for the GMT
Items.Abstract: We are developing the SuperFIRE concept, which builds on the heritage of the FIRE spectrograph at Magellan, as a UVOIR natural seeing spectrograph for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) with support from the Kavli Foundation. This single-object spectrograph is envisioned as a first-light instrument that can operate in natural seeing and grow in long-term capability as the telescope and AO systems mature. Here we discuss how the science case and design have evolved since the concept was initially conceived and presented at SPIE in Edinburgh ten years ago. Deep science drives the design goals to higher spectral resolution (R=10,000) and broader wavelength coverage (u through K bands) to complement JWST observations and fast low-noise detectors (LmAPDs and skipper CCDs) to reach sky limited performance in short integrations to follow up e.g. Rubin and Roman transients.

Items.Authors: Janice Houston
Items.Title: Designing the Black Hole Explorer: a systems engineering approach
Items.Abstract: The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) is a submillimeter VLBI space mission concept led by the Center for Astrophysics as the Principal Investigator institution and developed by the broader BHEX collaboration. Building on the Event Horizon Telescope’s images of two supermassive black holes, BHEX aims to uncover new physics through studies of photon rings, jet dynamics, and black hole populations.    The mission operates an orbiting BHEX radio instrument with ground-based observatories to form a single virtual telescope with an effective aperture larger than Earth. High-speed optical communications enable downlink of the mission’s large science data volume, and mission implementation combines traditional spacecraft operations with data-intensive science activities.    This technical overview describes the BHEX mission’s flight and ground systems and outlines the systems engineering approach used across the collaboration.

Items.Authors: Akira Endo, Tom J. L. C. Bakx, Jochem J. A. Baselmans, Dries Boleij, Stefanie A. Brackenhoff, Bernhard R. Brandl, Martino Calvo, Shahab O. Dabironezare, Hans van der Does, Rei Enokiya, Sho Fujisawa, Shinji Fujita, Enrico Garaldi, Wouter Gregoor, Masato Hagimoto, Davit Hakobyan, Angelina Harke-Hosemann, Robert Huiting, Shiro Ikeda, Reinier M. J. Janssen, Kenichi Karatsu, Nick de Keijzer, Kotaro Kohno, Takumi Kojima, Alkistis Kyriakidou, Louis H. Marting, Tomotake Matsumura, Cory Meijneke, Tetsuhiro Minamidani, Arend Moerman, Kana Moriwaki, Alessandro Monfardini, Kanako Narita, Yuri Nishimura, Erika Ogata, Leon G. G. Olde Scholtenhuis, Tristan Oude Essink, Jim R. Piek, Matus Rybak, Kana Sakaguri, Seiichi Sakamoto, Aurora Simionescu, Nikita A. Soshnin, Tatsuya Takekoshi, Yoichi Tamura, Akio Taniguchi, David J. Thoen, Sten Vollebregt, Lingyu Wang, Paul P. van der Werf, Stephen J. C. Yates, Naoki Yoshida, Silvia Zhang
Items.Title: Development of TIFUUN: terahertz integral field units with universal nanotechnology
Items.Abstract: SUBLIME (Study of the Universe By Line Intensity Mapping Experiments) is a new LIM experiment that aims to map [CII] emission at redshift 5.0–8.7 to trace the cosmic large-scale structure and the buildup of galaxies during reionization, using the integral-field spectrometer TIFUUN on the ASTE 10-m telescope. TIFUUN uses arrays of spaxels (spatial pixels), each of which is an integrated superconducting spectrometer, extending the DESHIMA concept to a compact dual-IFU system that has no moving parts. The two IFUs simultaneously cover 130–178 GHz with 19 spaxels and 195–319 GHz with 61 spaxels, with spectral resolution R ≈ 100–500. We present the system design and current hardware development of TIFUUN, including cryogenics, opticals, on-chip filterbank, and the miniaturization of kinetic inductance detectors to increase detector density. We also show forecast sensitivities for the SUBLIME–TIFUUN survey and outline future development pathways toward facilities such as FYST and AtLAST.

Items.Authors: Timothy R. White, Connor Langford, Max Charles, Louis Desdoigts, Thomas Holland, Patrick Oppel, Michael Lynch, Karel Valenta, Christopher Betters, Peter Tuthill
Items.Title: Edge data processing and control software for the TOLIMAN space telescope
Items.Abstract: The TOLIMAN Space Telescope is a University of Sydney-led project aiming to discover Earth-sized planets in the Alpha Centauri AB binary. The telescope has a novel diffractive pupil design that will allow the detection of tiny changes in the positions of the stars in the system, down to a millionth of a pixel in scale. Among the challenges for this low-cost mission are the stringent pointing requirements and data volume. The innovative piezo-driven tip-tilt system will receive attitude data from the payload sensor at 100 Hz, with science images taken at 10 Hz, generating 5 TB/day of raw data. However, the mission will only be able to down-link approximately 7 GB/day. Here we present our software solutions to these challenges, with real-time data processing to ensure pointing stability, with compression by a factor of 1000 while minimizing information loss to reach the science requirements within the thermal, power, and data budgets of the mission.

Items.Authors: Nimesh A. Patel, Satoki Matsushita, Derek Kubo, Tirupati K. Sridharan, Ramprasad Rao, Philippe Raffin, Rema Jamal Ahmid, Pierre Martin-Cocher, Chih-Wei Huang, Keiichi Asada, Cristina Romero-Canizales, Chih-Chiang Han, Yau-De Huang, Shu-Hao Chang, Jun Yi Koay, Ming-Tang Chen, Pai-An Chen, Jia-Ruei Nian, Ta-Shun Wei, Steve Leiker, Peter Oshiro, Sally Lau, Jacob Hawthorne, Keara Carter, Timothy Norton, Sheperd Doeleman, Jose Soto, Hannah Rana, Thomas R. Greve, Paul Ho
Items.Title: Near-field holography system for the Greenland Telescope
Items.Abstract: We describe a near-field holography system for the 12-m Greenland  Telescope (GLT) for dish surface error measurements. A 94.5 GHz  beacon on South Mountain ridge (2.8 km) is scanned using the 86 GHz  receiver and a reference receiver behind the subreflector to measure  beam-pattern amplitude and phase. The far-field pattern is corrected  for the phase-reference-plane locations of the receivers due to  movements relative to the pivot point during scanning. The near-field  correction is applied after Fourier transformation to the aperture  plane. Phase unwrapping, when needed, enables least-squares fitting  and removal of large-scale aberrations (dc, tilt, defocus, coma),  yielding surface-error maps. A Python pipeline based on the SMA  HOLIS package performs the reduction. The holography’s 14 cm  aperture-plane resolution improves on photogrammetry by a factor  of four, and the surface rms errors (~40 µm) are comparable between  methods.

Items.Authors: Marcell Westsik, Carolyn Atkins, Marta Civitani, Gabriele Vecchi, Katherine Morris
Items.Title: Lightweight 3D-printed fused silica mirrors for X-ray astronomy: design, analysis, and manufacture
Items.Abstract: Combining high spatial resolution imaging with low-mass mirrors for X-ray observatories is challenging. Recent advances in 3D-printed Fused Silica may address this challenge by enabling engineers to incorporate lightweight lattice designs – Triply Periodic Minimum Surface (TPMS) and Voronoi lattices – into the grazing incidence mirrors, whilst advances in polishing may provide sub-nanometre RMS surface roughness. We designed and optimised a grazing-incidence mirror segment (100×100 mm, 244.5mm radius of curvature) in three variants: solid, TPMS, and Voronoi. Using Finite Element Analysis we optimised the lattice parameters, and achieved a mass reduction of 37% with the TPMS and 29% with the Voronoi latticed samples. The printed samples were polished and characterized, demonstrating the feasibility of 3D-printed lightweight optics for the next generation of X-ray observatories.

Items.Authors: Anna Francesca Pala, Florian Kerber, Alain Smette, Michael Abdul-Masih, Angel Otarola, Omar Sqalli, Cyrielle Opitom
Items.Title: Characterisation of the atmospheric total ozone column over La Silla Paranal Observatory
Items.Abstract: The coming instruments CUBES (at the Very Large Telescope, VLT) and METIS (at the Extremely Large Telescope, ELT) of the European Southern Observatory (ESO) will be particularly sensitive in spectral regions strongly affected by absorption processes due to ozone, one of the trace gases in Earth's atmosphere. Characterising total ozone is hence crucial to optimise science operations and maximise the scientific return of these facilities. We present a method to derive total ozone and assess its night-time variability at the ESO’s sites with a precision of ~2%, using spectroscopic data of stars routinely used to spectro-photometrically calibrate the observations. This study will help determine whether twilight observations of standard stars can deliver ozone measurements accurate enough to correct telluric lines in science spectra, thus reducing the need for additional calibrations and enabling a more efficient and flexible observatory schedule across a wide range of observing conditions.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo Zago, Laurent Jolissaint
Items.Title: Comprehensive modeling and sizing tool for medium size segmented mirror telescopes
Items.Abstract: Segmented primary mirrors are increasingly considered for medium-size (4-m) ground-based telescopes,  offering advantages in cost, mass, and thermal behavior.   We present OPTICA (Optical Performance of a Telescope Including Correction with Adaptive optics), a Python  analytical tool for computing the image quality of segmented mirror telescopes.   OPTICA exploits an exact factorization of the system OTF into multiplicative contributions from segment errors, Zernike aberrations of all mirrors, high-order surface errors, seeing and AO correction.   Each complete case takes a few seconds.  The tool is specifically designed for: (i) fast exploration of telescope design space; (ii) telescope and AO system error budgeting; (iii) understanding dominant trade-offs and building physical intuition on key design aspects; (iv) first-order assessment of AO correction; and (v) first-order interpretation of test results.  Its application to an 18-segment, 4-m telescope is illustrated, with and without AO.

Items.Authors: Biao Zhao, Yasuhiro Hirahara, Seiichi Hata, Yuan Li, Chenhao Zhao, Shohi Negishi, Yuki Ashikari, Ryoichi Koga, Kasaba Yasumasa, Hideo Matsuhara, Shunsuke Baba, Umi Enokidani, Takao Nakagawa, Fumiyuki Ito, Takehiko Wada
Items.Title: Development of a wide‑band imaging FT‑IR using wavefront‑division interferometry for future planetary and space‑exploration payloads
Items.Abstract: We aim to obtain two-dimensional, spatially resolved infrared spectra for compact planetary and small-satellite missions. To meet this goal, we developed an imaging FT-IR spectrometer that uses wavefront-division Fourier interferometry and Zernike freeform mirrors. The instrument covers 4–20 µm with 3.8 cm^-1 wavenumber resolution and 34 µm spatial resolution. An uncooled mid-infrared camera records an interferogram and a spectrum at each pixel, so a full 2D spectral map is acquired in one scan. Extended sources reduce spatial coherence and wash out the fringes. We address this by placing a slit-array Wavefront Pre-Selection Mask module (WPSM) at the entrance plane. The WPSM raises the center-burst amplitude of 50 and nearly doubles the fringe contrast. A 960 cm^-1 quantum cascade laser test shows a mean wavenumber offset of 0.05 cm^-1, and polystyrene standard data agree with catalog spectra, showing that this system can provide accurate 2D infrared spectra.

Items.Authors: Tim Hardy, Erning Zhao, Greg Burley
Items.Title: Initial characterization of the 512x512 pixel SaphiraQM infrared APD array.
Items.Abstract: We present our results from the initial testing and characterization of the 512x512 pixel SaphiraQM infrared APD detector from Leonardo. This sensor is optimised for wavefront sensing and has 64 high-speed outputs. We developed custom electronics to enable operation of the device at its full rated speed of 10 Mpixels/s per output, or more than 2,000 frames/s.

Items.Authors: Michelle J. Creech-Eakman, Van Romero
Items.Title: Magdalena Ridge Observatory Interferometer: first fringes and next steps for the imaging facility
Items.Abstract: The Magdalena Ridge Observatory Interferometer (MROI) is located in central NM at 10,500 ft. altitude. It is the most ambitious imaging optical interferometer being built today, with an ultimate design capable of supporting 10 movable telescopes operating at optical/NIR wavelengths, and baselines from 8 to 347 m. We have recently reached the milestone of first fringes, and within a few nights of observations attained 8.9 magnitudes at H-band. In this invited talk, we will present end-to-end technical performance of the system and discuss where we anticipate making improvements in the coming year. MROI expects to begin installing the third telescope/beamline by the summer of 2026, all funded through the Air Force Research Lab in Albuquerque, NM. Plans for new instrumentation and early scientific observations will be presented. We are actively pursuing new funding for future beamlines and telescopes and are open to partnering opportunities for the facility.

Items.Authors: Kobus Cloete, Fernando Camilo, Scarre Celliers, Willem Esterhuyse, Hans-Rainer Klöckner, Michael Kramer, Pontsho Maruping, Keitumetse Molamu, Sean Passmoor, Grazia Maria Umana, Gundolf Wieching
Items.Title: Status update on the extension of the MeerKAT radio telescope
Items.Abstract: The construction phase of the MeerKAT Extension (MK+) project, which extends the current MeerKAT array at the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO) site in the Karoo region of South Africa, is nearing completion. We will provide details and updates on the construction and early engineering commissioning results. The South African MeerKAT telescope is a SARAO precursor to the Square Kilometre Array mid-frequency instrument (SKA-MID). The MK+ project is a partnership between SARAO, the Max Planck Society (MPG, MPIfR), and the Istituto Nazionale di Astrofisica (INAF), and is an important milestone towards the SKA-MID array.

Items.Authors: François Leroux, Cédric-Taïssir Héritier Salama, Christophe Vérinaud, Markus Kasper, Thierry Fusco, Benoît Neichel
Items.Title: The bi-o-edge wavefront sensor: from the laboratory validation towards its on-sky deployment
Items.Abstract: We report on the latest development obtained with the Bi-O Edge Wave-Front Sensor, a candidate for future eXtreme Adaptive Optics instruments with its very high sensitivity that outperform the modulated pyramid with no price to pay in terms of dynamic range. We present the results obtained in lab with the first Bi-O edge implementation based on the use of patterned liquid crystal technology to perform the Fourier Filtering modulating the polarization of the light. This communication reports on the validation of the Bi-O Edge gain in sensitivity as well as the demonstration of its super-resolution capabilities.

Items.Authors: Thomas Pfrommer, Lorenzo Pettazzi, Steffan Lewis, Jose Antonio Abad Pastorino, Constanza Araujo Hauck, Helen Bedigan, Pierre Bourget, Martin Brinkmann, Elsa Calmette, Greidy Castellanos, Angela Cortes, Byron Engler, Christoph Frank, Fernando Gago Rodriguez, Elizabeth George, Thomas Grudzien, Ivan Maria Guidolin, Andreas Haimerl, Peter Hammersley, Marcus Haug, Stefan Huber, Paul Jolley, Aglaé Kellerer, Manuel Kern, Mario J. Kiekebusch, Jean-Paul Kirchbauer, Barbara Klein, Johannes Kolmeder, Johan Kosmalski, David Kosten, Paolo La Penna, Ulrich Lampater, Serban Leveratto, Ignacio L. Gil, Christopher Mandla, Enrico Marchetti, Leander H. Mehrgan, Christophe Moins, Jérôme Paufique, Oliver Pfuhl, Dan Popovic, Malte Scherbarth, Babak Sedghi, Sébastien Tordo, Sara Zuccon, Pablo Zuluaga-Ramírez, Petr Janout, Eduardo Garces
Items.Title: The ELT Phasing and Diagnostic Station: system overview and status before system tests
Items.Abstract: The ELT Phasing and Diagnostic Station (PDS) is the measuring tool that provides the necessary data, enabling the commissioning team to locate and shape all telescope mirrors to nominal position, including phasing the ELT primary mirror. This brings the ELT to diffraction-limited performance and into operational configuration for science by verifying telescope performance with respect to the high-level specifications.   PDS is designed, developed, and built internally at ESO and has currently finished the integration and assembly phase, which included opto-mechanical assembly and optical alignment. This was followed by subsystem testing and performance verification using the final and verified electronics and control software, deploying the ELT instrument framework. The project is about to enter system testing with a fully assembled PDS system, after the planned test readiness review this fall 2026.

Items.Authors: Ivan Rodriguez Ferrandez, Sanath Muret, Leonidas Kosmidis
Items.Title: Accelerating space-instrument data processing: benefits of on-board gpus for scientific missions
Items.Abstract: Future space missions generate data volumes that exceed downlink limits, making efficient on-board processing  essential. Radiation-tested embedded GPUs offer high parallel performance and low power consumption, well  suited to space systems. We evaluate three GPU-accelerated instrument pipelines on an NVIDIA Orin NX:  the OBPMark #1.1 wide-field optical calibration and correction pipeline, the Euclid NIR preprocessing chain  for cosmic-ray removal and calibration, and the THESEUS XGIS coded-mask imaging and transient-detection  algorithm. The calibration pipeline saturates around 665–670 Mpix/s and the NIR chain peaks at 799 Mpix/s  at full-focal-plane scale, both within a 6.5 W module budget, while XGIS sky-image reconstruction completes  in 0.562 ms, roughly 1480× faster than an optimized CPU implementation. These results show that a single  radiation-tested embedded GPU can deliver reliable, high-throughput, low-latency processing for next-generation  scientific missions.
